content.p: The Grim Reapers Motorcycle Club began in Calgary in 1967 and ended in 1997, when its members put on Hells Angels colours at a ceremony in Red Deer. In between, the club left a trail in the Canadian courts. A death on a highway south-east of Calgary in 1970 produced a murder trial and a Supreme Court of Canada ruling, and a feud with a rival club in the 1980s produced bombings, beatings, a disappearance and a provincial court judgment on what counts as an "outlaw motorcycle gang". The final chapter was a legal fight over a 1997 traffic stop, which former members won on appeal in 2005, according to the biker-history site One Percenter Bikers.

Much of what is recorded about the club comes from two kinds of page, which differ in reliability. Court documents give the 1970 killing and the 1988 hearing in sober, checkable terms. A hobbyist chronology gives most of the 1980s feud, and it often says only that a club was "suspected". Where a claim rests on that chronology, this account says so. It is also easy to confuse this club with the Grim Reapers formed in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1965; One Percenter Bikers states that the two are unrelated.
content.h2: A Calgary club of the late 1960s
content.p: One Percenter Bikers puts the founding in Calgary in 1967, by a group who liked riding Harley-Davidsons, and calls it the first "one percenter" club in the city. The Rebels, it says, appeared in 1969, and it links King's Crew as the other club that followed; the King's Crew page puts that club's founding at around 1977. In the 1980s, the same site says, the Grim Reapers were one of four main clubs in the Calgary area, alongside the Rebels, the Warlords and King's Crew. By the end of that decade, its King's Crew profile adds, three clubs remained as the main outlaw groups in Alberta: King's Crew, the Grim Reapers and the Rebels.

The phrase "one percenter" has a disputed history. The CBC explains that the American Motorcyclist Association said in the 1960s that 99 per cent of riders and their clubs were law-abiding, leaving a hard-partying one per cent. The Outlaws club told the broadcaster that police changed the meaning in the 1980s so that it came to describe members of criminal gangs. The Outlaws, it says, still wear their one percenter patches proudly.

The earliest event in the club's record here is also its most thoroughly documented, because it reached the Supreme Court of Canada. The court's judgment in Emkeit v. R., written by Mr Justice Ritchie for the majority, describes two gangs of young people from in and around Calgary. One was the Outcasts. The other carried the name of the Grim Reapers, and all of the accused but two belonged to it.

According to Ritchie's summary, there had been bad blood between the groups, and some of those involved hoped a meeting might sort out their differences. The two sides arranged to meet at 8 p.m. on 7 March 1970 at Little Rock, roughly 15 miles south-east of Calgary. Some of the Grim Reapers came armed with bull whips and logging chains, while the Outcasts carried no weapons. The Grim Reapers, in four cars, arrived first, found nobody and set off back towards Calgary. Very soon they met the Outcasts, who travelled in a car and a panel truck with six girls, one of them Ronald Hartley's wife.

What happened next comes from Mrs Hartley's account as the court recounts it. A man later identified as Ronald Emkeit got out onto the highway and asked who the president of the Outcasts was. When Hartley said it was he, he was told to get out of the car and was struck on the side of the head with a chain. Hartley said, "God man, why?" Hartley then could not drive, stiffened and began to lose the use of his body. He was laid on a mattress in the panel truck and driven towards the hospital with mouth-to-mouth resuscitation attempted on the way. He was breathing for most of the journey but was dead on arrival. Mrs Hartley described the weapon as a logging chain with one-inch links. A fight then broke out around the truck. The passage the court quotes, in which the speaker is not named, says that everything around it "just exploded" with "fighting and screaming and hollering".

Thirteen young men, Emkeit among them, were tried together before Mr Justice Primrose and a jury on a charge of non-capital murder. The indictment accused each of them of forming a common intention to assault people with offensive weapons, knowing or ought to have known that murder would be a probable consequence. All were convicted.

The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Alberta then reviewed the verdicts and split the outcome. It acquitted one of the accused and ordered new trials for everyone except Emkeit, whose conviction it upheld. The reasons for that difference are not in the judgment, so they are not reconstructed here. One Percenter Bikers gives a shorter version of the aftermath: 11 members and 2 associates were sentenced to life, and after appeals some were released and others had their sentences reduced, leaving two members convicted and serving life. The Supreme Court's judgment does not give sentences or the later fate of those who were retried, so that account stands alone and should be read as the hobby site's summary.
content.h2: Emkeit's own version, and a poem read to the jury
content.p: Emkeit was the only accused who testified. As the Supreme Court quotes him, he said he had asked the man who he was, that Hartley replied that he was president of the Outcasts, and that Emkeit "kind of snickered". According to Emkeit, Hartley took a swing and missed, Emkeit pushed him against the car door, and as Hartley came back at him Emkeit swung a chrome chain he wore round his neck. He said he moved in to hit him again but did not, because Hartley raised his hands and said "No more". The self-defence claim was put to the jury. Mr Justice Ritchie wrote that, even accepting that Hartley took a swing, Emkeit's own words admitted that he had hit an unarmed man about the head with a chrome chain and that the man died of the beating.

The appeal to the Supreme Court turned on something else. Near the end of cross-examination, Crown counsel asked Emkeit whether a man named George Lowe was a poet and then read to the jury a club poem called "Grim Reapers". The verse spoke of citizens who scream and daughters who should beware, of "Satan's spawn", and ended with lines of obscenity about the world and "hell is their fate". None of the eight defence counsel objected as it was read, but soon afterwards they asked the judge to discharge the jury, after 26 witnesses over three days. Primrose refused, telling the jury that the poem was not evidence and was not "a statement of the aims of the Grim Reapers".

Counsel for Alberta conceded in the Supreme Court that the poem was inadmissible, as both the majority and the dissent record. The question was whether the jury should have been discharged. Four judges (Abbott, Judson, Ritchie and Pigeon) said no. Their reasoning was that a trial judge has a wide discretion, that the poem advocated nothing like the assault Emkeit had himself admitted, and that no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice had occurred. Three judges (Hall, Spence and Laskin) dissented, finding Emkeit had been seriously prejudiced by what they called the "incomprehensible conduct" of Crown counsel. The appeal was dismissed.

The feud that followed is told mainly in the chronologies of One Percenter Bikers, whose King's Crew and Grim Reapers pages largely mirror each other. Its entries are brief and many are expressed as suspicion, so they should be read as allegations. The site says the long conflict with King's Crew ran through the 1980s and brought "multiple beatings and murders".

In November 1980, the site says, Grim Reapers arrived armed at the Lethbridge clubhouse of the Ghost Riders and forced the club to hand over its colours. In February 1983 five sets of King's Crew colours were taken at gunpoint by Grim Reapers; they were burned and delivered to the offices of the Calgary Sun. In March rifle shots were fired into the Grim Reapers' Calgary clubhouse, an act the King's Crew profile says was believed to be the work of King's Crew. The King's Crew clubhouse was bombed on 13 April 1983 and destroyed, and on 27 April its president Melvin Jordan's home was bombed and then shot at fifteen times.

On 16 May 1983 a vehicle belonging to a Grim Reaper was bombed. The two pages disagree about whose it was. The Grim Reapers page names Dennis Bullen's truck, while the King's Crew page names Larry Graham's car, and the latter also lists a Larry Graham as a King's Crew member who was pistol-whipped in an attempted kidnapping with his wife on 8 June. Ronald Moore of King's Crew was killed on 10 June 1983 when his jeep, booby-trapped, exploded as he tried to start it. On 30 July the Southside Harley and Speed shop in Edmonton, owned by Grim Reapers according to both pages, was bombed; the King's Crew page says King's Crew members were suspected.

Violence continued against individuals. On 18 December 1983, according to the King's Crew page, a member named James St Pierre was admitted to hospital with multiple stab wounds, which it says were suspected to be the Grim Reapers' work. On 22 January 1984 Steven Albert Joell was shot outside his home and later died, with the Grim Reapers suspected. In April 1984 a King's Crew member named Wayne Jordan, confronted outside a convenience store by two Grim Reapers with a shotgun, ran inside and called the police, who arrested the men he named; King's Crew then expelled him for informing. On 13 August 1984 a Grim Reapers member, David Worshek, was badly beaten by King's Crew members.

On 26 July 1987, the chronologies say, three Grim Reapers (Michael Doll, Kerry Eastman and Derek Smith) beat a King's Crew member unconscious and took his colours. The pages spell his surname differently, as Doyes and as Moyes, and this account does not choose between them. On 1 October 1987 Valerie Blatt reported her husband, King's Crew member Louis Aaron Blatt, missing. The King's Crew page says that it was suspected that the Grim Reapers kidnapped and killed him and disposed of the body, possibly so that the club could not claim a $50,000 life insurance payout. The Grim Reapers page says only that members were suspected of kidnapping and murder. Neither page reports a charge, and nothing in these sources shows what became of the investigation, so the allegation stays unproven here.
content.h2: The courts define an outlaw gang, 1988
content.p: Police had meanwhile seized firearms and other articles from members of both clubs. The members applied under section 101 of the Criminal Code to decide what happened to the seized items. The matter came before Judge Pepler of the Alberta Provincial Court, who delivered his decision on 26 August 1988. The reported headnote refers to at least 135 paragraphs of reasons, with paragraphs 1 to 127 discussing what an "outlaw motorcycle gang" is.

The judge held that, on a section 101 application, the burden of proof on the balance of probabilities stayed with the Crown, but that the Crown could meet it simply by establishing that the applicants were members of outlaw motorcycle gangs. He stated that such a ruling did not infringe freedom of association under section 2(d) of the Charter. The headnote records orders to dispose of many of the seized articles and to bar several members from holding firearms and similar items for some years. The headnote does not say which members, or from which club.
content.h2: Becoming Hells Angels, and the 2005 appeals
content.p: In 1997, One Percenter Bikers says, the Hells Angels patched over the Grim Reapers at a ceremony in Red Deer, taking in a total of 23 members. They formed the Edmonton and Calgary chapters, which the site calls the 13th and 14th Hells Angels chapters in Canada. The timing was tense. The Hells Angels were then at war in Quebec with the Rock Machine, a conflict the site dates from 1994 to 2002. The CBC describes the war as a turf struggle that claimed more than 150 lives, among them two prison guards and 11-year-old Daniel Desrochers, killed when a car bomb exploded outside a biker hangout. Public outrage at his death prompted Bill C-95, the 1997 law that stiffened penalties for convicted offenders shown to be members of established criminal organisations.

One Percenter Bikers lists a former Grim Reaper, Gerry Weldon, who joined in 1973 and later became president of the Hells Angels' Edmonton chapter, as the one member noteworthy in biker history. The site says the club had no "famous" members otherwise.

The same site reports that in 2005 multiple former Grim Reapers, by then in Hells Angels chapters in western Canada, won on appeal in cases arising from a 1997 traffic stop made under powers created by Bill C-95. It gives no court, judge or case name, and none of the pages opened here reports the ruling in detail, so the legal reasoning is not given. Other coverage of the new law was more cautious. The CBC reported that Criminal Intelligence Service Canada's 2004 report said the law seemed to be having an effect, and that the Hells Angels were "experiencing varying degrees of weakness in Alberta, Manitoba, Quebec and Atlantic Canada".
